## Open

### F-167 — Seed ordering: dbTest assets run before another realms production seeds

> _2026-09-16 · realm/blong-access · open_

A dbTest seed in blong-party could not resolve the access Admin role (unknown access.role Admin)
even though the access realm loads first: the party realm dbTest batch is processed before the
access realms production meta/db seeds. Lesson: a dbTest seed may only reference what it creates
itself, or what a file it runs after creates. The ACL grants were moved into
realm/blong-party/meta/dbTest/accessAuthorizationMerge.yaml, which creates the role it grants to (9-
prefix for the hierarchy, a- for the RBAC/ACL file).

### F-169 — Errors matched via .expect lose params.reason in the ACL flow test

> _2026-09-16 · realm/blong-access · open_

The session tests read the failure reason from error.params.reason and pass, but in the new party
ACL flow the reason came back empty while the type was correct (the adapter-raised and realm-raised
errors both carry params.reason). The ACL test therefore asserts error types only. Worth
understanding before relying on reason-based branching in tests.

### F-170 — Second action resource for one action silently disabled the ACL rule

> _2026-09-16 · realm/blong-access · open_

The ACL matrix wrote partyPersonEdit while the seeds had registered party.person.edit; the deny then
had no effect and the flow failed with 'the matrix rule denies the write'. The DB showed two action
rows for one logical action. Fixed by matching on the dot-stripped name (aclActionResourceId) and
reading both name shapes (aclActionParts). Lesson: never create a graph resource that a
pattern-based lookup resolves - reuse what exists.

### F-174 — The ACL matrix never rendered its stored rules

> _2026-09-16 · realm/blong-access · open_

The pivot matches a stored row to its dropdown option on the join fields, label included, so an
option labelled 'all: (all records)' never matched a read row carrying the bare
core_resource.resourceName '(all records)'. Every stored rule rendered as an empty row and the edit
phase could not even release it (the blank cell was already at the wanted state, so no click was
made). resourceLabel() is now shared by resourceOptions and aclMatrixRows; the -tab-matrix-open
capture proves load. A read handler must emit the joined label exactly as the dropdown builds it.

### F-312 — A pivot ticks whichever row the database happens to return first

> _2026-09-28 · realm/blong-access · open_

The role spec's capability pivot ticks the `granted` cell of the first row, and the pivot renders
the whole dropdown in whatever order the database returns it: one run granted guestBasic and the
next granted accessModelAdmin, and the difference (5303 pixels of a 1.44M-pixel capture, 0.37%)
stayed inside the diff tolerance, so the baseline kept showing the wrong row while every run passed.
This is T-173's defect in its second instance; the fix is a filterable column plus a named row, and
a third instance is still open in capability.play.ts's action pivot. Lesson: a pivot capture is only
evidence when the spec names the row it toggles, because the tolerance that makes these captures
robust to fonts and antialiasing is far wider than a checkmark in the wrong row. Same shape as F-115
and F-298: a shared, ordered list where the spec assumed an order.

### F-315 — A rebuild that runs before the last delete leaves a grant behind

> _2026-09-29 · realm/blong-access · open_

Removing a capability deleted its hasAction edges, rebuilt the paths, and only then deleted the
hasCapability edges that grant it to roles — so the roles that had been granted it kept the
capability's actions in their flattened paths until something else happened to rebuild, and nothing
recorded that they were stale. The direction matters: a stale path here grants an action whose
capability no longer exists. It stayed invisible because every deletion the specs perform is
followed by further writes that rebuild, and because the two statements sat next to each other
looking like one operation. The lesson is the ordering rule rather than the feature: when a write
and the rebuild that derives from it are not in one transaction, the rebuild goes last and covers
everything the write did — and 'a rebuild ran' is not the same claim as 'a rebuild covered this
change', which is the distinction the generation and covered counters exist to make.

### F-343 — A role held directly and inherited from the unit crashed the path refresh

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-access · open_

access_pathRefresh failed at startup with a duplicate primary key on core_path when a subject held a
role that its unit also held: access_effectiveRolePath reports that (subject, role) pair twice, once
at depth 1 and once at depth 2, and core_path is keyed by originId, destinationId and pathType, so
the second row cannot be inserted. The rebuild now groups by that key and takes MIN(pathDepth), as
its scope CTE already did. An additive test seed that only inserts edges makes this easy to hit,
because a stale edge left by an earlier run is enough — the fixture seeds now delete the edges they
own before merging.

## Resolved

### F-296 — The gateway does not read the paths the RBAC pages say it reads

> _2026-09-27 · realm/blong-access · resolved_

Verification for two posts caught three claims that had been repeated across the RBAC documentation.
The authorization hook queries core_triple directly, joining hasCapability and hasAction, and never
reads the materialized core_path paths - those are read at login, where the per bitmask is built
from access.effectiveRole, and by access.session.verify from access.effectiveAction. So 'a decision
is one indexed lookup instead of a recursive walk' describes login rather than the per-request
check. 'No database round-trip on the hot path' holds only while a 30-second per-caller cache is
warm. And 'a freed bit is never reused' is false for the highest bit in use, because allocation is
MAX + 1: deleting that role hands its bit to the next one. The lesson is that a claim about where a
query happens is as testable as a claim about its result, and it is the kind of claim that survives
review because it reads like a summary.

Corrected the stale claims wherever they were repeated: realm/blong-access/README.md, the RBAC
rationale, the gateway concept, the 2026-07-05 post, the blong-core skill, and the role-bit comments
in error.ts, accessRoleEnsure.ts and 1-accessRoleMerge.yaml. Verified against the code:
accessAuthorizationList joins core_triple with a 30s per-bit cache, accessPermissionList and
accessSessionVerify read core_path, and allocation is MAX + 1.

### F-297 — The ACL documentation promised a deny that the guard can ignore

> _2026-09-27 · realm/blong-access · resolved_

The record-level ACL is documented as 'a deny always wins', but the combined filter is (unscoped OR
guarded) and the unscoped term short-circuits for a record that participates in no scope, so a
record-targeted deny on such a record is not applied. The same term is what makes mode scoped safe
to adopt, so the two properties are one mechanism described twice, once as a guarantee and once as a
convenience. Three other statements were wrong in the same area: a capability cannot be a principal
because the filter resolves the caller, their effective roles and their units and never a
capability, so such a rule is inert; targetKind 'all' exists in code and in the seeded data but was
missing from the README field list; and 'no materialized table to invalidate' ignored that the
verdict reads access.effectiveScope and access.effectiveRole, so a hierarchy change still needs
access_pathRefresh(). Corrected in the concept, pattern and rationale pages, the realm README and
the schema comments.

The concept and pattern pages already carried the hole; brought the realm README, the ACL rationale,
the ACL schema comments, the gogo acl comments (server/acl.ts, schema/knex/types.ts) and the
blong-core skill in line, and dropped the capability-as-principal wording. mode explicit's
deny-by-default and targetKind all are now stated everywhere.
